subtitulo: Conquest, imperial synthesis, and the conversion of Hellenism into a contested resource (336 – 323 BCE, and 1991 – 2026)

coda.heading: Coda for the journey: what to look for

items.text: First, pay attention to vocabulary. Listen to how naturally the word HELLENISM is used in Greece to designate not a historical period but a transnational, timeless community that includes the diaspora. It is an active political category, not an academic term, and it functions as a resource for mobilization and claim-making. Compare it with the way "the Andean" or "the Inca" is used in Peru: also designations that do political work in the present and are not innocent as to who falls inside and who falls outside.

Second, in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens, look for the Hellenistic and post-classical representations and observe the change in visual regime: from the idealized, serene body of the fifth century, one moves to the individualized portrait, to pathos, to gesture, to old age and pain represented. It is not merely stylistic evolution. It is the emergence of the individual as a legitimate subject of representation at a time when the political community had ceased to be the frame of meaning. When the polis stops deciding, art discovers biography. It is a regularity that recurs in any society where the collective horizon closes.

Third, a warning. The figure of Alexander is the most contaminated in this series: appropriated by British imperialism as a forerunner, by Greek nationalism as a founder, by corporate management as a case study in leadership. Treat him for what he was: an eleven-year episode that destroyed an empire, did not fully replace it, and left a vacuum that others would administer. The next installment examines exactly that: how the successor generals turned that vacuum into the first international system of dynastic states, how Alexandria became the intellectual center of the world, and how Greek became the lingua franca of empires that were no longer Greek — the condition that defines, to this day, the cultural elites of the periphery.

sections.heading: A poorly framed question: was Alexander Greek?
paragraphs: It is worth defusing, from the outset, the question that has poisoned two centuries of Balkan historiography. Asking whether the Macedonians "were Greek" projects onto the fourth century BCE a category — modern ethnic nationality — that did not exist. What did exist was a repertoire of partial, contested criteria of belonging: language, cult, participation in the panhellenic sanctuaries, the right to compete at Olympia, and above all the gaze of others. The Macedonian kings claimed Argive descent and competed in the games; Demosthenes, in the Third Philippic, called Philip a barbarian, not even worthy of being a respectable slave. Both things were true in their own register: Macedonia was culturally Hellenic at court and structurally foreign to the world of the poleis, because it was a territorial monarchy with an equestrian aristocracy and a dependent peasantry — that is, a type of society that Athens associated with Persia and not with itself.

The relevance of this discussion is not antiquarian. Between 1991 and 2018, the Republic of Macedonia and Greece sustained a diplomatic conflict that blocked accessions to NATO and the European Union, mobilized more than a million people in the streets of Greece in 1992 and 2018, and was resolved only with the PRESPA AGREEMENT of June 2018, which fixed the name North Macedonia in exchange for the lifting of the Greek veto. The agreement cost Alexis Tsipras his government and remains contested by sectors on both sides; in May 2024, the new Macedonian president omitted the constitutional name from her oath of office and reopened the friction, which continues unresolved in 2026. A proper name from twenty-three centuries ago still functions as a geopolitical resource. No society that has argued over the ownership of pisco, the denomination of the potato, or the use of the term "Inca" in international marketing can consider this quaint: disputes over symbolic patrimony are disputes over the capacity to convert memory into sovereignty and into money.

sections.heading: The campaign as process, not as epic (334–330 BCE)
paragraphs: Alexander crosses the Hellespont in 334 BCE with about thirty-five thousand men and a considerable debt. Formally he leads a panhellenic war of vengeance decreed by the League of Corinth; materially, he needs the Persian treasury to avoid bankruptcy. The three decisive battles — the Granicus in 334, Issus in 333, Gaugamela in 331 BCE — are usually narrated as a demonstration of military genius, and they were. But the most revealing element is what happens between the battles.

In 332 BCE, Tyre resists for seven months; Alexander builds a causeway from the mainland to the island, takes the city, executes thousands, and sells the rest into slavery. Gaza receives similar treatment. This is not youthful excess: it is calculated terror policy, designed to produce rapid surrenders along the rest of the Phoenician coast and to deprive the Persian fleet of ports. Conquest is administered with a deliberate economy of exemplary violence, a calculation any scholar of state violence will recognize, and one that reappears in the Spanish conquest of the Andes: Cajamarca in 1532 operates with the same logic of a terrifying spectacle aimed at an audience far larger than the victims present.

And yet, alongside the terror, there is administrative continuity. In Egypt, in 331 BCE, Alexander is crowned according to pharaonic rite and visits the oracle of Amun at Siwa. In Babylon he respects local cults and orders the rebuilding of the temple of Marduk that Xerxes had damaged. He keeps Persian satraps in their posts, preserves the Achaemenid fiscal structure, adopts elements of court ceremonial. The image of the Hellenizer imposing civilization upon barbarism is a later construction, largely nineteenth-century and colonial: what Alexander does, above all, is CAPTURE A STATE APPARATUS that functioned better than anything Greece had ever produced, and place himself at its apex. Persepolis burns in 330 BCE — a drunken accident or a calculated symbolic act, the sources disagree — and with it the pretext of panhellenic revenge is cancelled. From then on, the war is no longer Greek: it is the construction of an empire of his own.

sections.heading: The problem of governing: how does one rule over diversity
paragraphs: The internal tensions within the Macedonian army between 330 and 324 BCE are, in sociological terms, the richest episode of the entire campaign, because they display the conflict between two incompatible legitimacies. Traditional Macedonian monarchy was a kingship of companions: the king was first among equals, drank with his nobles, could be argued with. Persian kingship was an institution of sacred distance, with the gesture of PROSKYNESIS — reverence before the sovereign — as obligatory protocol. When Alexander attempts to introduce it around 327 BCE, the Macedonians read it as the worship of a man, something reserved for gods, and refuse. The historian Callisthenes, nephew of Aristotle, leads the objection and dies shortly afterward under obscure circumstances. Before him Philotas had fallen, and Parmenion himself was assassinated on the king's order; and at Samarkand, in 328, Alexander killed with his own hand Cleitus the Black, who had saved his life at the Granicus, during a drunken argument over whether his achievements were his own or his father's.

The easy reading is megalomaniacal degeneration. The useful reading is different: Alexander was attempting to solve, with no precedent and no manual, the central problem of every multiethnic empire — how to produce a common legitimacy for populations with incompatible criteria of authority — and the cost was paid by the cadres of the conquering core, who demanded to keep the privilege of familiarity. The Susa weddings of 324 BCE, at which he married some eighty officers to Iranian noblewomen and ten thousand soldiers to Asian women, and the training of thirty thousand young Persians in the Macedonian phalanx, provoked the mutiny at Opis that same year. The veterans were not protesting on principle: they were protesting because they were being made replaceable.

That conflict — between a conquering elite that demands exclusivity and a power that needs to broaden its base by incorporating the conquered — recurs with remarkable fidelity in the viceroyalty of Peru. The tensions between encomenderos and the Crown, creole resistance to Bourbon administration, the debate over the place of indigenous elites and the status of the mestizo, are variations on the same structural dilemma. And the imperial response tends to be the same: the center needs to mix in order to govern, and the center's local agents resist mixing because their position depends on the frontier. When Alexander dies in Babylon in June 323 BCE, at thirty-two, he leaves the problem completely unresolved.

sections.heading: The other Alexander: Epirus, the Ionian, and the gaze toward the West
paragraphs: There is a second Alexander in this story, and his systematic omission distorts the map. Alexander I of Epirus, called the Molossian, was uncle and brother-in-law to the conqueror — brother of Olympias, married to a daughter of Philip. While his nephew crossed into Asia, he crossed the Adriatic toward Italy in 334 BCE, summoned by the Greek city of Tarentum to fight the Italic peoples, and died in battle at Pandosia around 331 BCE. There is even an ancient report, transmitted by Livy, of a treaty between him and Rome.

That two members of the same house march simultaneously east and west shows that the Greek world of the fourth century conceived of two horizons of expansion, not one. And the starting point of the western horizon is exactly the strait separating Epirus from Corcyra: Corfu lies barely two kilometers from the mainland coast at its nearest point, and Paxos sits immediately to the south, along the route. When in September you stand in Corfu town looking toward the mainland — those Albanian and Epirote mountains visible from the Esplanade — you will be looking at the platform from which the Hellenic world attempted to project itself onto Italy two centuries before Rome projected itself onto Greece. The history of domination is read better from the straits than from the capitals: in the strait you can see the direction of the flow, and see when it reverses.

sections.heading: The simultaneous world: Chandragupta, Rome, Carthage, the Andes
paragraphs: Alexander's conquest does not occur in an empty world. His incursion into the Punjab in 326 BCE — and the mutiny at the Hyphasis, where his army simply refused to advance any further, the only real limit he encountered — coincides with the formation of the Maurya empire: Chandragupta takes Magadha around 322/321 BCE and, around 305, negotiates a treaty with Seleucus that cedes him the eastern satrapies in exchange for five hundred war elephants. That is: the Hellenistic expansion halts not from its own exhaustion but from the simultaneous rise of a comparable empire on the subcontinent. In China, the state of Qin advances toward the unification it will complete in 221 BCE. In Italy, Rome fights the Samnite Wars that will give it the center of the peninsula. In the western Mediterranean, Carthage dominates trade.

In the Andes, this is the period of consolidation of the regional traditions that followed Chavin: Paracas Necropolis, the first developments of Nasca and Moche. None of these societies produced a conquest empire in this era; Andean unification will arrive with Wari and later with the Tahuantinsuyo. But the contrast illuminates something important about Alexander himself: the lightning conquest was possible because a unified Persian empire already existed, with roads, a postal system, a cadastre, and a treasury, ready to be decapitated and occupied. A conqueror does not create an apparatus of government in eleven years; he inherits one. It is exactly what Pizarro will do in 1532 with the Inca apparatus, in an even shorter span and with an even smaller army. Rapid conquest is not proof of civilizational superiority: it is proof that a centralized state architecture existed whose capture at the summit was enough to inherit the whole. Societies without a center — the jungle peoples, the Illyrians, the Scythians — proved far harder to conquer and were never fully subdued.

sections.heading: Resonances 2024–2026: the name, the marble, and the identity commodity
paragraphs: Alexander's contemporary legacy is less military than patrimonial, and that is where it becomes concrete. Greece sustains simultaneously three fronts of dispute over its own past. The first is that of North Macedonia, already described, frozen since Prespa but reactivated in 2024 and still open in 2026, in a context in which the Balkan expansion of the European Union is stalled and the influence of other outside actors grows in the vacuum.

The second is that of the Parthenon marbles, whose negotiation between Athens and the British Museum ran through 2023–2026 with formulas of "cultural partnership" and rotating loans that avoid pronouncing on ownership. Greece maintains, correctly, that the object is not just any movable good but a constitutive part of a monument and of a national genealogy. The same argumentative structure sustains the Peruvian claims to the Machu Picchu pieces held at Yale, resolved in 2011 with a return that was simultaneously a diplomatic victory and a confirmation of asymmetry: return happens when the possessor decides to return.

The third, less visible and more determinant, is the conversion of the past into an economic flow. The "Alexander the Great" brand structures tourism in northern Greece, the airport of Thessaloniki bears his name, and a monumental statue has presided since 2014 over the central square of Skopje, erected by a government that invested hundreds of millions in an operation of architectural antiquization of the capital. In both cases the past is not preserved: it is produced, with public funds, to sustain a narrative and an income. The Peruvian comparison is immediate and requires no delicacy: the dispute over access to Machu Picchu, ticket sales, transportation concessions, and the regional strikes of 2023 to 2025 over who administers entry to the sanctuary are exactly the same thing. Heritage is a rent, and where there is rent there is distributive conflict dressed up as identity conflict.
